questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go on exchange to explore topics within my field that weren't available to me at UCPH (mostly de- and postcolonial theory as well as just basic gender studies). But I got a lot more than academic insight from the exchange in terms of personal development, friendships, and nature experiences.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The only cons were a roomie who smoked indoors and the amount of assessment in the Canadian educational system.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. UBC's Go Global office is very informative. You receive emails throughout the months before arrival with all sorts of information preparing you for the upcoming exchange. You can also always reach out to both Go Global and the instructors by email and they'll be happy to answer all your questions.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I don't remember receiving anything in particular because I didn't need anything. But there were a lot of offers and opportunities to seek help fx through course and career counseling, mindfulness and stress management, and conflict resolution if you were having difficulties with your roomies.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Canadian students are generally younger than in the Danish higher educational system and therefore there's a lot of help to get just in general. The students are "treated" as young people who might not have that much experience with adult life. It can feel a bit condescending at times but it helped me to just think of the constant checking in as a gift you can accept but don't have to.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: There are several on-campus housing options available at UBC. I was lucky to get a room in Fairview which is a small collection of townhouses where I shared my everyday life with other local and international students. It feels like living in a small secluded village close to campus (20 min stroll from the center of campus). There's a cafe where you can study and you greet the other students when you pass them on the street. The houses are pretty worn out and not in the best shape, but that's North American house building for you... Other on-campus housing opportunities include Walter Gage where some of the other exchange students I knew lived. That's more modern housing. Eight-story apartments with a view of the mountains and the ocean. About 50% of the exchange students got on-campus housing as far as I recall.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There were meal plans available but I didn't want that (didn't look that good tbh), and also I love to cook. It's important to know that when moving into on-campus housing there is NO kitchen equipment. There are appliances like an oven, stove, microwave, and fridge, but you have to buy plates, bowls, glasses, cutlery, pots, pans, whatever you need to cook.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about on campus housing? *
questions.answer: The same goes for stuff in your room! No comforter, pillows, bed sheets, or hangers. So a trip to IKEA is the first thing on the to-do list when arriving. Otherwise, the UBC Bookstore has some complete sets for your bed and the convenience stores on campus can help out as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Soundproofing is non-existent and the houses are just in general very old and - but that being said I felt so lucky living there and having a sense of community and not being afraid of scams or dealing with overpriced housing.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: You'll get walked through by email. And also there was an opportunity to join a Zoom meeting (recordings sent out afterward) with detailed descriptions of the registration process.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You're emailed all the necessary information from Go Global! The deadlines are different from what's written on the website but don't stress. You have to choose 10 prioritized courses that don't overlap (as far as it's possible) and you'll get appointed five of those. But due to the drop period in September, you have almost a whole month where you can still browse courses and go to lectures even if you have not registered.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Again, Go Global is your friend.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Completely successful. I got four out of four wished courses. But my field is also kind of niche, so I'm lucky that way.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If there's a course that's restricted or full or whatever - don't despair. Try to engage in conversation with the professors, send emails, or show up at the lectures. The system is way more flexible than they (UCPH and UBC) tell us. Also, when it comes to specific fields of research that we're told we can't study. I think the whole anthropology section is noted down as inaccessible for exchange students which ended up being not entirely true. Talk to people and stay curious. There are a lot of possibilities if you're creative.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of interesting courses to choose from and the professors are generally passionate and experts in their fields.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: There are courses on levels between 100 and 500 (100-level courses being suitable for first-year students, 200 for the second year, and so forth). I took four 400-level courses. Initially, I wanted to take 500-level courses but you can't apply for those before you arrive, and by that time I was way too occupied with just finding my way through exchange and didn't want the fuss of changing schedules. And I was also happy with my choices.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It's quite different. Self-study is not a thing in the anglo-saxon education system. There might be mandatory attendance and the workload during the semester is quite heavy compared to UCPH. Depending on your courses more or less is expected of you, but I was required weekly to turn in assignments, complete quizzes, do presentations, and bring forth discussion questions. And then of course there are midterm exams, midterm essays, peer assessments, and exams. But it's important to stress that failing is fairly difficult and you can actually not turn stuff in or not show up for a test and still get a well-about average grade. I wish I'd known that.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1) Colonialism and After
2) Religious Feminisms
3) Sociology of the Environment
4) Gender and Nation: Women's State in Modern Central, Eastern and Northern European Literatures and Cultures

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Colonialism and After might be one of the most important courses I've ever taken. Dr. Pierre is an expert in her field, and even though the lecturers were very hard-core in terms of difficult, violent, and sensitive subject matter it really turned my worldview around. Dr. Meadows who taught Sociology of the Environment is without a doubt the most engaging professor I've ever encountered in academia. I highly recommend everyone to take that course as well.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Housing before moving into permanent residence cost me an additional 5000DKK. And even though public transportation is free when you're a student I did spend quite a lot on busses (16DKK pr. trip) before being officially enrolled. And I spent a looot more money on weekend trips and vacations than planed, but no regrets there.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Groceries are crazy expensive in Vancouver!!! And the taxes are high. So everyday shopping is expensive. And there's a liquor tax as well which will hit you hard if you like drinks...

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: 10/10. There are more than 500 student clubs at UBC so everyone will be able to find a community if they want. And there's free entrance at the swimming pool which is a plus.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: All of them... Painting, baking, yoga, political discussion groups, sports, varsity outdoor club, climbing, skiing and snowboarding, surfing. You won't miss anything.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking... Just go hiking. What UBC and Vancouver has going on for them is the sorrundings. And they're near perfect. Find someone to enjoy the nature with.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go hiking in Garibaldi Provincial Park (as well as just the Squamish area in general), go skiing or snowboarding in Whistler, and visit Vancouver Island for surfing and/or swimming and just enjoying the coastline. If you have more time I highly recommend the Canadian Rockies and North Cascades in Washington State.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Yes in general. Canada is a Western country and the people are very much like Danish. They're just more polite and open and extroverted. They will for sure approach you and try to engage in conversation even if you haven't initiated contact.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Be as open-minded and polite as the people you meet and you will have no problem finding a lot of friends. And try not only talking with the other Danes. It can be a challenge because it's much easier to just stay within your comfort zone, but the international friends I got really taught me a lot and I wouldn't have had the same amazing time without getting to know them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Only the fact that when the cashier greets you with a "Hi, how are you" they do not expect you to elaborate on your feelings.... Just answer "Good thanks, how are you"....

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The kindness and the openness.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Don't worry too much about passing your courses - you will. Prioritize a multitude of experiences in addition to the academic ones 
2) Say yes to all the outdoor experiences you can get. If someone invites you kayakking - you go.
3) Even though it's easier to joust make friends with the other Danes, stay curious and get to know as many internationals as possible

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't worry too much about the grading. It can seem overwhelming to get marks on every single assignment quiz or presentation, but in the end, that won't be what you remember.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The international friends that I made and the nature experiences.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: One of my roomies smoking inside for sure, but we handled it. And I was always in a position to ask for help if needed. Otherwise, the stressing out about exams and midterms and assignments and what not - which is why I'm trying to stress that you shouldn't!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go! You won't regret it.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
